*HDS MSc · Module 3 · the R version of this exercise; the web page is at <https://inflamuob.github.io/HDS_M3/day9/day6-04-subgroups.html>.*

*Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time. Keep it in the folder that holds your `data` folder. Cells with `______` are blanks for you to fill in.*

> **A suggested addition, not part of the original module**
>
> This exercise has no page in the original version of the module. Exercises
> 9.1 to 9.3 explain the model as a whole and one patient at a time; this one
> asks whether it works equally well for different groups of patients. Accept,
> rewrite or remove it; nothing else depends on it.

One test AUC describes the model for all the test patients together. The
model can still serve some groups much worse than others, and the overall
number will not show it. Here we split the test patients by age and by BMI and
compare.

> **The plots are for looking at**
>
> The code for every plot is included, so that you can run it and see the figure. You are not expected to write it yourself.

### The model

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

The same data ([`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv)) and
random forest as Exercises 9.1 to 9.3. As always, 80% of the people are used
for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))
```

Evaluate it once on all the test rows (threshold 0.5):

```{r}
class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, sens)
class_metrics(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

Accuracy 0.720, sensitivity 0.618, AUC 0.753. These are the overall numbers
we will now break down.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — Performance by age group

Put the test patients into three age groups. For each group, count the
patients, the patients with diabetes and how many of those the model catches,
then work out the accuracy and the sensitivity.

```{r}
test_preds <- test_preds |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(age, breaks = c(20, 29, 39, Inf),
                         labels = c("21-29", "30-39", "40 and over")))

test_preds |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(patients = n(),
            with_diabetes = sum(diabetes == "pos"),
            caught = sum(diabetes == "pos" & .pred_class == "pos"),
            accuracy = mean(.pred_class == diabetes),
            sensitivity = caught / with_diabetes)
```

yardstick's functions also work on grouped data, one row per group. The AUC
for each age group:

```{r}
test_preds |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

**Question!** Which age group does the model serve worst?

It depends on the measure. In the youngest group the accuracy looks fine
(0.750), but the model catches only 9 of the 24 people with diabetes
(sensitivity 0.375); most young people do not have diabetes, so being right
about them keeps the accuracy up. In the oldest group it catches 15 of 19, but
it has the lowest accuracy (0.588) and an AUC of 0.558, close to the 0.5 of a
coin toss. None of this shows in the overall numbers.

The plot shows the predicted probabilities in each age group, split by whether
the patient really has diabetes. Most of the young people with diabetes sit
below the 0.5 line.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
test_preds |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = .pred_pos, colour = diabetes)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, seed = 1), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "Predicted probability of diabetes", colour = "Diabetes")
```

### Part 2 — By BMI, and how far to trust a small group

**Your turn.** Do the same with two BMI groups: under 30, and 30 or over (the
usual cut-off for obesity).

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
test_preds <- test_preds |>
  mutate(bmi_group = if_else(mass < ______, "under 30", "30 and over"))

test_preds |>
  group_by(bmi_group) |>
  summarise(patients = n(),
            with_diabetes = sum(diabetes == "pos"),
            caught = sum(diabetes == "pos" & .pred_class == "pos"),
            accuracy = mean(.pred_class == diabetes),
            sensitivity = caught / with_diabetes)

test_preds |>
  group_by(______) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

> **Stuck?**
>
> BMI is the column `mass`, and the cut-off is 30. Group by the new column,
> `bmi_group`.

**How far can we trust these numbers?** The sensitivity of 0.364 in the
BMI-under-30 group rests on 11 people: 4 caught out of 11. One more caught
would make it 0.455, one fewer 0.273. With so few people, one patient moves
the number a long way, and a different random split could tell a different
story. Differences between small groups are a reason to look again with more
data, not a finding. That is why the counts always go beside the metrics.

> **Key points**
>
> - The overall numbers can hide large differences between groups of patients.
> - Which group looks worst depends on the measure: accuracy, sensitivity and AUC answer different questions.
> - Always report how many patients, and how many with the outcome, each group's numbers rest on. A few people give unstable numbers.
